claims.text: Equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni is a single-phase fcc alloy.
Equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni has established high-temperature and cryogenic mechanical properties.
Small changes in Al content alter atomic-size mismatch in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
Al-induced changes in atomic-size mismatch produce corresponding changes in mixing enthalpy.
Atomic-size mismatch and mixing enthalpy govern fcc-solid-solution stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
Composition-dependent thermodynamic effects can determine the temperature range over which an fcc solid solution is stable.
Increasing Al content causes greater lattice distortion.
Increasing Al content makes the mixing enthalpy more negative.
The Al-induced thermodynamic changes can stabilize or destabilize the fcc phase depending on temperature and environmental conditions.
Changes in Al content will systematically shift phase-transformation temperatures or phase fractions relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Al-dependent phase-stability shifts will correlate with high-temperature yield strength and cryogenic ductility or toughness.
Phase boundaries controlled by the proposed mechanism underlie high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Phase fractions and unit-cell changes can be assessed using X-ray diffraction.
An fcc-to-hcp transition is a relevant possible phase transformation in the proposed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni comparison.
Within a modest Al-composition window, elemental segregation and other processing-induced effects will be minimal.
Extreme Al deviations or processing conditions may activate mechanisms not captured by atomic-size mismatch and mixing enthalpy.
Radiation-induced defects may interact with compositional tuning in ways not explained solely by atomic-size mismatch and mixing enthalpy.

contradictions.description: Changing the Al atomic fraction while holding all four other elemental concentrations constant is not compositionally well-defined under normalized atomic percentages; the non-Al fractions must change or the total will no longer sum to 100%.
